comments.author: mpyne
comments.text:
OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration.
The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password.
The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login.
The bug is from the intersection of all of these things:
1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”.
2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards.
3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user l

comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
The whole story is a bit worse than this.  Musl
already worked around this type of failure
.  See the second-to-last line here:
https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_des...
(hey, this workaround is wrong if the salt is "x"!)
but they forgot to work around it here:
https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha...
The vulnerable path in musl is only a little bit vulnerable, because "*" is not actually a
sha256
encrypted configuration and should not reach this code: musl's crypt(..., "*") will not call that code!  Turns out that sshd detects that the password hash is too short
and does not forward the salt
!
https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/auth...
Look, no else statement!  If that if doesn't get taken, then salt remains NULL.  And the sshd code is really quite messy and doesn't keep track of the fact that this code path is inappropriate for validating an existing password hash.
A workaround in the sha256 path in musl wouldn't even have prevented the bug!
I'm going to give some credit to musl for unwisely using "*" and some credit to OpenSSH for having nonsensical control and data flow.

comments.author: aljgz
comments.text:
My general rule of thumb is: "no magic strings". This is much easier to implement in higher-level languages and when writing application/web code than system programming.
Don't return empty string/asterisk/anything else. Instead, return a failure value.
When absolutely needed, choose the magic string with more caution:
One string showing the SHA-256 of a non-existing hash? It's a good idea for it to be a valid hash. Now we have a new risk: if it's broken once, it's broken for all. So it's a good idea for it to be a random one for each machine and/or account. Even this might have problems I can't think of, but it seems to be as secure as an account with a real password.
If this is not a good decision for some reason, choose something unmistakable: "--ACCOUNT-HAS-NO-PASSWORD--". This is much less likely to be mistakenly used in a different context, is much easier to look up in a code base than "*", and is self-documenting.

comments.author: NewJazz
comments.text:
musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.
Does anyone know why musl does this? Are they the only C library that behaves this way?
For a C library that famously tries to adhere to POSIX as much as possible, this seems like a crazy choice. From POSIX standard:
Upon successful completion, crypt() shall return a pointer to the encoded string. The first two bytes of the returned value shall be those of the salt argument. Otherwise, it shall return a null pointer and set errno to indicate the error.
https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/c...

IMO this is where languages like Rust shine. The design patterns built into the language for handling errors (Result) - force you to handle errors / function results with sentinels, null pointers, or errnos are so much more error prone than handling a Result<T,E> using a match statement.
crypt() returning `*` is insane especially since these kinds of sentinels are all over /etc/passwd

comments.author: xms17189
comments.text:
Fascinating architecture—treating agent turns as persistent lightweight actors backed by tiered SQLite/S3 rather than spinning up dedicated VMs makes a lot of sense for latency and cost.
For workflows that inevitably require arbitrary shell execution or local compiler tools (like coding agents running tests), do you envision delegating just the side-effect execution out to ephemeral runners while keeping the stateful actor long-lived, or is Rivet primarily focused on API/tool-calling agents?

comments.author: kianN
comments.text:
> When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.
As someone who is not incredibly deep in the agent space, but works a lot on scientific and distributed computing, this really caught my eye. Seems like this is primarily part of the cloud offering, but a true posix compatible filesystem that interops cleanly with S3 on the backend would be an incredibly interesting product (especially if it were open-sourced).
A brief sidenote: I did a triple take when I saw the name because Rivet is the internal name of our long-running job queue service. You all have great taste.

stories.title_en: Goodbye from Salon

comments.author: legitster
comments.text:
The amount of newsroom jobs fell 60% between 2008 and 2020. The vast majority of what was lost were "beat" reporters - foreign bureaus, Washington bureaus from regional publications, statehouse reporters, or regional specialty beats (science, law, etc).
This started long before the decline of the open internet and AI. If anything, the shift online covered up a massive hollowing out of the industry. We're getting fewer sources of news, and more national coverage. A lot of stuff that is reported on is coming from a scant number of wire services, or directly from PR teams themselves.
For the most part, your choice of news platform is just a layer of coverage choices and political spin on top of a very thin market of original coverage.

I wouldn't normally describe hearing a voice as hearing "vibrations". Vibrations are indeed the physical basis of sound, and the auditory system detects changes in air pressure caused by them. stories.title_en: The Stacks Project, Formalized in Lean

comments.author: QuesnayJr
comments.text:
After they announced the formalization of the classification of Finite Simple Groups, I immediately wondered "What would happen if you tried to formalize the Stacks Project?"  Despite also being very long, it's the opposite of the CFSG: instead of a poorly organized set of results that contribute to proving one big theorem, it's instead a carefully-organized set of results that cover a broad area.
The Stacks Project was the model for how mathematics should be done (at least for the pre-LLM era).  Algebraic geometry had lots of poorly organized foundational results that were not really created for themselves, but in order to solve problems in the field.  One person, Aise Johan de Jong, set out to fix it by organizing a project to write out the proofs of all of the results in a carefully organized fashion.  He's led the project since, though of course there are multiple contributors.  The whole thing is thousands of pages.
I would be interested in hearing more about the gaps they uncovered in the existing results, and how they fixed them.

I understand the allure of doing this kind of work in AI on some level, but I'm becoming increasingly skeptical of generating "knowledge" that's difficult or impossible for humans to understand (at scale or otherwise).
